prompt: How many integer values of $x$ satisfy $-3 < \dfrac{x - 4}{2} \le 1$?
hint: First find the range of $x$ by working on all three parts together. Then count the whole numbers in that range, watching the two ends.

hints.text: First find the range of $x$ by working on all three parts together. Then count the whole numbers in that range, watching the two ends.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try counting on a small range: $0 < x \le 3$ holds for $x = 1, 2, 3$ — three integers. The strict end excludes its boundary, the inclusive end keeps it.
Multiply all three parts by $2$ to get $-6 < x - 4 \le 2$, then add $4$ to get $-2 < x \le 6$. Decide which end value is included.
The value $-2$ is excluded and $6$ is included, so the integers run from $-1$ to $6$. That makes $8$ integer values.

learningObjective: Solve a compound inequality and count the integers in the solution set.
explanation: Multiply all three parts by $2$ to clear the denominator: $-6 < x - 4 \le 2$.
Add $4$ to all three parts to isolate $x$: $-2 < x \le 6$.
The left sign is strict, so $-2$ does not count and the smallest integer is $-1$. The right sign allows equality, so $6$ counts.
The integers $-1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6$ satisfy the inequality, so there are $8$ integer values.

alternativeExplanations.title: Counting integers without slipping
steps: From $a$ to $b$ inclusive there are $b - a + 1$ integers — the "+1" is what people forget.
Here the range is $-1$ to $6$, so $6 - (-1) + 1 = 8$.
Listing them out is also fine when the range is short; it is the safest check on a fencepost error.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: Forgetting the +1 gives 7; miscounting the strict end brings −2 into the list and gives 9.
Write the two boundary integers explicitly — smallest −1, largest 6 — then count with b − a + 1. The formula only works after the ends are settled.
